Liberty Walk Founder Says This Tuned Ferrari F40 Is His Favorite Car. Do You Dig the Makeover?
6 photos
Photo: Instagram | libertywalkkato
The Ferrari F40 may have been dead and buried for three decades, but it continues to make headlines today, and you can understand why, can’t you?
If you said no, then you may want to throw away your petrolhead license, as you clearly do not use it. This model remains a motoring icon, and it is one of the best vehicles the Prancing Horse has ever made. On top of that, it is the last model approved by Enzo Ferrari himself before he passed away in 1988.
Ferrari’s F40 may look quite modern on the outside, but it was actually developed in the 1980s. It hit the production line back in 1987 at the Maranello factory in Italy, and was discontinued 9 years later, in 1996, after over 1,300 units were put together. The number includes the GTE, Competizione, and LM models.
Designed by Pietro Camardella under the close watch of Aldo Brovarone at Pininfarina, with Nicola Materazzi being the chief engineer, the supercar was offered in a single body style, a two-door berlinetta. The coupe had a longitudinally-mounted engine mounted in the middle toward the rear, right behind the passenger compartment, which drove the rear wheels through a five-speed manual transmission.
Photo: Instagram | libertywalkkato Given that it was born in the 1980s, some might think that the Ferrari F40 could feature a V12, or perhaps a V8 with no forced induction. But it actually features twin turbocharging, and if you know your classic supercars, then you remember that the mill of choice had a 2.9-liter displacement, pumping out 471 hp (352 kW/478 ps) and 426 lb-ft (577 Nm) of torque.
According to the spec sheet, the 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 kph) acceleration took just 4.1 seconds, which is highly impressive for something that it almost four decades old. Flat-out, the F40 did 201 mph (324 kph), and if you are curious about the standing quarter mile, then you should know that it completed it in 11.9 seconds.
Alongside the 288 GTO, the F50, Enzo, and LaFerrari, the Ferrari F40 is considered to be one of the best machines ever signed by the Prancing Horse. Something like this usually fetches between $2.5 and $5.5 million in today’s market, and an ultra-low-mileage example changed hands for over $8.3 million recently.
As a result, the Ferrari F40 is not exactly the kind of car that deserves to get a tuning job. However, that does not mean that there are no modified examples out there, because some of them have been visited by the tuning fairy, including the one pictured in the gallery, which has got to be one of the most famous tuned F40s out there.
Mind you, it’s not a new project, because it has been around for quite a few years now, and we have dedicated several stories to it so far. And as it happens, this machine recently smiled for the camera again, with the images being shared on social media by Liberty Walk’s founder recently, who admitted that this is his favorite car.
Photo: Instagram | libertywalkkato We can understand why, because the Ferrari F40 remains a dream machine, though purists will likely not agree with the widebody makeover. The fender flares, new lip attached to the front bumper, some extras at the rear, a large diffuser, and a big rear wing, alongside a set of beefy side skirts, make up the aftermarket redesign.
This thing also has three center-mounted exhaust tips that are bigger than the OEM ones, a retuned suspension, new wheels, and a white look sprinkled with some decals. The interior is home to red bucket seats and some other extras, and some might argue that it rocks this design perfectly, whereas others would definitely agree to disagree.
The purist crowd may definitely want to look away, because they would describe this build using one word: sacrilege. Or perhaps a synonym of that word. However, the attention to detail is definitely there, and to be honest, it would not take that much to revert this Ferrari F40 back to its original condition.
I’ve always had a soft spot for most things Liberty Walk, and while this tuner’s builds may usually follow the same widebody, stanced recipe, it is this exact bundle that has made them famous. Therefore, while I would probably want to hate this modified Ferrari F40 , I simply can’t, because to me, it looks almost perfect. After all, what’s wrong with a widebody classic exotic model that sits closer to the ground and rides on new wheels?
This comment will probably spark some hate toward me in the comments area, but hey, we all have our soft spots and simple pleasures when it comes to the car game, don’t we? That said, feel free to speak your mind below about this tuned Ferrari F40, regardless of whether you hate it or love it. But honestly, do you really hate it?
